# Quick start

Lookup tables explain the codes used in the gnfi data. They associate a code with a label and, depending on the table, additional information.
For example, the federal-state code `8` represents Baden-Württemberg.

Use `view_lookup()` to retrieve a lookup table from the REST API. Choose the
table with the `table` argument: `table = "state"` retrieves the federal-state
lookup, while `table = "tree_species"` retrieves tree-species definitions. The
same function provides data viewing and export options for every lookup table.

```{r quick-start, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
library(gnfidatR)

# Retrieve the federal-state lookup and open it in the data viewer:
view_lookup(table = "state")

# Retrieve the same lookup for use in a script:
federal_states <- view_lookup(table = "state", view_data = FALSE)
head(federal_states)
```

Pass the table name **without the `lookup_` prefix**. The function adds it
internally, so `table = "state"` queries the API table `lookup_state`. Use the
exact values listed in the [table reference](#table-reference).

By default, `view_lookup()` opens `utils::View()` and also returns the result
invisibly. Assign the call to a variable to keep the data; set
`view_data = FALSE` when you do not want to open the viewer.

The examples in this vignette are shown **without being executed** during the
build and are excluded from the extracted vignette script. Run them manually
with internet access to query the API, open a viewer, or create export files.

# Arguments and behaviour

`view_lookup()` retrieves data through `gnfi_query()`. It selects all columns
from the chosen table in the `lookup` API schema and requests rows ordered by
`code`, then `id`. It does not select an inventory cycle automatically; check
the returned `interval` values when interpreting historical codes.

| Argument        | Default                            | Purpose                                                                                                      |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `table`         | Required                           | One lookup name without `lookup_`, for example `"state"` or `"tree_species"`. See the table reference below. |
| `url`           | `"https://ci.thuenen.de/rest/v1/"` | REST API base URL.                                                                                           |
| `apikey`        | Included public key                | API key passed to `gnfi_query()`; supply a different key when needed.                                        |
| `page_size`     | `-1`                               | Value passed to the `limit` argument of `gnfi_query()`; its interpretation is handled there.                 |
| `create_csv`    | `FALSE`                            | Enable CSV export through `gnfi_query()`.                                                                    |
| `csv_name`      | `NULL`                             | CSV file name or path, interpreted by `gnfi_query()`.                                                        |
| `create_sqlite` | `FALSE`                            | Enable SQLite export through `gnfi_query()`.                                                                 |
| `sqlite_name`   | `NULL`                             | SQLite database file name or path, interpreted by `gnfi_query()`.                                            |
| `sqlite_table`  | `NULL`                             | Table name within the SQLite database.                                                                       |
| `view_data`     | `TRUE`                             | Open `utils::View()`; use `FALSE` in scripts or when knitting.                                               |

The result is the object returned by `gnfi_query(return_data = TRUE)`, returned
invisibly. You can assign it to a variable whether or not the viewer is opened.
To inspect the complete function signature in R, use `args(view_lookup)`.

## View a result with a custom title

The default viewer title is derived from the lookup name: `"land_use"` becomes
`"Land Use"`. To choose your own title, retrieve the data first and open the
viewer yourself:

```{r named-view, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
land_use <- view_lookup(table = "land_use", view_data = FALSE)
utils::View(land_use, title = "Land use categories")
```

## Export a result

Enable CSV or SQLite export with the corresponding arguments. The result is
still returned, so you can keep it in R while exporting it:

```{r export-examples, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
marker_profile <- view_lookup(
  table = "marker_profile",
  create_csv = TRUE,
  csv_name = "marker_profile.csv",
  view_data = FALSE
)

view_lookup(
  table = "harvest_method",
  create_sqlite = TRUE,
  sqlite_name = "lookups.sqlite",
  sqlite_table = "harvest_method",
  view_data = FALSE
)
```

# Reading lookup tables

Lookup tables contain **code definitions**, not inventory observations or
counts. Most tables have the following structure:

| Column     | Meaning                                                                                                      |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `code`     | Domain code used by inventory records; usually numeric, but text in the `interval` lookup.                   |
| `id`       | Internal UUID identifying the lookup row.                                                                    |
| `name_de`  | German label.                                                                                                |
| `name_en`  | English label, where available; some labels are missing or incomplete.                                       |
| `interval` | Inventory-cycle tags supplied by the source. Check them when interpreting historical codes.                  |
| `sort`     | Optional display-order value. `view_lookup()` requests ordering by `code` and `id`, rather than this column. |

Some tables add metadata or links, such as `abbreviation` in the `state`
lookup, `growth_region` in `growth_district`, and `code_district` in
`municipality`. When joining an inventory field documented as a lookup code,
match it to `code`, not `id`. Use the labels and inventory context to interpret
a value; codes such as cover classes are not direct measurements.

# Table reference

The following groups list 64 lookup tables. Pass any value from the first
column to `table`, without the `lookup_` prefix. For example, use
`view_lookup(table = "land_use")` for
land-use definitions or `view_lookup(table = "tree_species")` for tree-species
definitions.

Descriptions summarize the lookup values and their use in the inventory schema
and field comments.

## Inventory design, fieldwork, and relocation

| `table` value          | Meaning and use                                                                                                                                                               |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"accessibility"`      | Whether a plot can be visited, with reasons for restricted access such as dangerous terrain, dense vegetation, or access prohibitions.                                        |
| `"cluster_situation"`  | How a cluster falls within the survey area and sampling grid, including border situations that require a complete, partial, or omitted survey.                                |
| `"cluster_status"`     | The forest-related status of an inventory cluster: previously surveyed forest, newly established forest cluster, uncertain forest status, or different non-forest situations. |
| `"gnss_quality"`       | GNSS positioning and fix-quality classes, including differential and RTK solutions, invalid fixes, and other positioning methods.                                             |
| `"grid_density"`       | Sampling-grid categories and their spacing, including denser grid subsets and a category for unsystematic training clusters.                                                  |
| `"interval"`           | Inventory-cycle identifiers and labels, such as bwi2022 and ci2027. This table uses text codes; `view_lookup()` does not select an inventory cycle automatically.             |
| `"marker_profile"`     | Physical form or material of the permanent plot marker, such as round iron, T-profile iron, magnets, or combinations of marking aids.                                         |
| `"marker_status"`      | Whether the permanent plot marker was searched for, found again, replaced, or installed for the first time.                                                                   |
| `"object_type"`        | The inventory object a note refers to, such as a cluster, plot, sample tree, boundary, regeneration sample, or deadwood item.                                                 |
| `"sampling_stratum"`   | Regional sampling-intensification strata, combining state or area membership with the sampling-density history used in different inventories.                                 |
| `"support_point_type"` | Purpose of a relocation aid, for example an offset marker, landmark, survey starting point, or GNSS support point.                                                            |

## Forest and site classification

| `table` value               | Meaning and use                                                                                                                                                             |
| --------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"elevation_level"`         | Natural elevational vegetation zones, from lowland and hill zones through montane to high-montane or subalpine zones.                                                       |
| `"exploration_instruction"` | The forest-site mapping guideline or instruction system used for site classification. Entries include regional guideline editions and a category for sites without mapping. |
| `"ffh_forest_type"`         | FFH forest habitat types, including habitat codes and categories for no habitat type or an unclear preliminary assessment. Used for preliminary and field classifications.  |
| `"forest_community"`        | Potential natural forest communities associated with a site, such as beech, oak, or mixed forest communities.                                                               |
| `"forest_status"`           | Forest/non-forest classification at a plot, with distinctions for stocked forest land, temporarily unstocked land, other forest land, and inventory-specific special cases. |
| `"land_use"`                | Land-use categories recorded for the plot, including agricultural land, wetlands, water, settlement, transport, and other land uses.                                        |
| `"terrain_form"`            | Topographic form at the plot, such as a plain, valley, slope position, ridge, or plateau.                                                                                   |

## Ownership, management, and harvesting

| `table` value           | Meaning and use                                                                                                                                                         |
| ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"harvest_condition"`   | Technical suitability of the site for timber harvesting, including requirements for slope-adapted machinery or cable extraction and substantially difficult conditions. |
| `"harvest_method"`      | Harvest pattern: no harvesting, selective removals, or area-wide removals. Technical site suitability is described separately by `harvest_condition`.                   |
| `"harvest_reason"`      | Reason for harvesting: regular operations, storm damage, insects/drought, other disturbance, or an uncertain or unknown cause.                                          |
| `"harvest_restriction"` | Restrictions on timber use and the expected share of normal harvesting, including unrestricted use and situations where harvesting is prohibited or not expected.       |
| `"management_type"`     | Silvicultural management system, including even-aged high forest, selection forest, coppice with standards, coppice, and short-rotation plantations.                    |
| `"property_size_class"` | Forest-ownership holding size classes in hectares. The classes describe the ownership holding rather than the sampled plot area.                                        |
| `"property_type"`       | Forest ownership categories, including federal or state forest, corporate/public-body forest, private forest, and more detailed legal-form variants.                    |

## Stand structure and regeneration origin

| `table` value                     | Meaning and use                                                                                                                                                           |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"basal_area_factor"`             | Basal-area factors 1 and 2 used for angle-count sampling of stand-structure trees taller than 4 m.                                                                        |
| `"cover_percentage"`              | Coded cover/share classes, mainly in approximate ten-percentage-point steps, used for low-tree vegetation and species shares. Read the labels for the class bounds.       |
| `"layer"`                         | Layer categories for vegetation up to about 4 m, including main stocking, regeneration, residual stocking, and a sampling-circle category.                                |
| `"stand_development_phase"`       | Stand development and diameter classes, from pioneer/pole stages to large old timber. This is a stand classification, separate from individual regeneration size classes. |
| `"stand_layer"`                   | Vertical position or role of trees within a stand, such as main stand, understorey, overstorey, or regeneration under an existing canopy.                                 |
| `"stand_structure"`               | Vertical structure of the whole stand: one layer, two layers, or multiple layers/selection structure, with additional historical subdivisions.                            |
| `"trees_greater_4meter_mirrored"` | Mirroring method recorded for sampling trees taller than 4 m: none, relascope mirroring, or the walk-through method.                                                      |
| `"trees_less_4meter_origin"`      | Origin of the low-tree vegetation: natural regeneration, sowing, planting, coppice shoots, or an unclassifiable origin.                                                   |

## Tree attributes, damage, and deadwood

| `table` value          | Meaning and use                                                                                                                                                             |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"bark_condition"`     | Bark condition relevant to diameter measurement, including intact, missing, partly present, or bulging bark; the entries also describe associated measurement handling.     |
| `"browsing"`           | Browsing damage on regeneration, distinguishing undamaged plants and damage patterns involving terminal buds and lateral shoots. Definitions vary between inventory cycles. |
| `"damage_peel"`        | Bark-stripping damage categories for regeneration: none, recent damage with possible older damage, or older damage only.                                                    |
| `"dead_wood_type"`     | Physical form of a deadwood item, such as a standing tree, standing fragment, stump, lying stem, or harvesting residue.                                                     |
| `"decomposition"`      | Deadwood decay stages, ranging from undecomposed material through beginning and advanced decay to heavily decomposed wood.                                                  |
| `"pruning"`            | Whether a tree was pruned and the pruning-height class. Historical inventory cycles may use different height bands.                                                         |
| `"stem_breakage"`      | Stem/crown breakage class: no break, a broken top, or a larger crown break; the labels define the length distinction.                                                       |
| `"stem_form"`          | Stem form and continuity, including a stem extending into the crown, forking, or lack of a distinct single stem; historical codes also include older special cases.         |
| `"tree_size_class"`    | Size classes for regeneration and small trees, defined using height and/or diameter at breast height (DBH), with inventory-specific historical classes.                     |
| `"tree_species"`       | Tree-species codes and names used across tree, regeneration, stand-structure, and related records; the schema also provides genus/species and other species metadata.       |
| `"tree_species_group"` | Broad wood/species groups used for deadwood: conifers, broadleaves excluding oak, and oak.                                                                                  |
| `"tree_status"`        | Sample-tree history and status, including new or remeasured trees, removals, dead or missing trees, invalid samples, and exclusions from earlier inventories.               |

## Forest and stand boundaries

| `table` value             | Meaning and use                                                                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"edge_stand_difference"` | Stand-height and tree-species-share differences across a boundary; the classes describe why adjacent stands are distinguished.                                       |
| `"edge_status"`           | History and validity of a recorded boundary, including newly recorded, retained, retrospectively identified, no longer valid, or previously excluded boundaries.     |
| `"edge_type"`             | Boundary category combining the neighbouring land/stand situation with whether the boundary is new, applies retrospectively, or was retained from an earlier survey. |
| `"edge_type_deprecated"`  | Legacy boundary classes for older inventories, including outer/inner forest edges and stand boundaries. Retained to interpret historical records.                    |
| `"terrain"`               | Land cover or stand situation on the other side of a forest/stand boundary, such as cropland, grassland, water, woodland, or an adjacent stand.                      |

## Geographic, administrative, and conservation references

| `table` value               | Meaning and use                                                                                                                                                        |
| --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"biogeographische_region"` | Biogeographical region assigned to a plot: Atlantic, Continental, or Alpine.                                                                                           |
| `"biosphaere"`              | Codes and names of biosphere reserves, including a category for no biosphere-reserve membership.                                                                       |
| `"biotope"`                 | Protected forest-biotope categories, including regional categories and a no-special-protection entry; used to interpret the biotope classification recorded at a plot. |
| `"district"`                | Administrative district and urban-district codes/names. Municipalities refer to these codes through `code_district`.                                                   |
| `"ffh"`                     | Named FFH conservation sites and a no-site category. This identifies site membership; `ffh_forest_type` describes the forest habitat classification.                   |
| `"forest_office"`           | Forestry administrative office codes and names associated with plots.                                                                                                  |
| `"growth_district"`         | Forest ecological growth districts (Wuchsbezirke), linked to their broader growth regions through `growth_region`.                                                     |
| `"growth_region"`           | Forest ecological growth regions (Wuchsgebiete), providing the broader regional framework for growth districts.                                                        |
| `"municipality"`            | Official municipality codes and names, with a `code_district` reference to the containing administrative district.                                                     |
| `"national_park"`           | National-park codes and names, including a category for plots outside a national park.                                                                                 |
| `"natur_park"`              | Nature-park codes and names, including a category for plots outside a nature park. Nature parks and national parks use separate classifications.                       |
| `"natur_schutzgebiet"`      | Nature-reserve membership indicator. Codes distinguish no membership (0) from membership (1).                                                                          |
| `"state"`                   | German federal-state codes, names, and abbreviations, plus an outside-Germany category. Used for plot location and inventory responsibility.                           |
| `"vogel_schutzgebiet"`      | Bird-protection area codes and names, including a category for locations outside these areas.                                                                          |

# Troubleshooting

`view_lookup()` uses `gnfi_query()` to retrieve a lookup table and, by default,
opens the result in a data viewer. If the function does not return the expected
data, first retrieve the table without opening the viewer:

```{r lookup-without-viewer, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
library(gnfidatR)

federal_states <- view_lookup(table = "state", view_data = FALSE)
head(federal_states)
```

If this returns the expected data, the download has succeeded. You can use the
returned object directly, even if the viewer is unavailable in your R session.

To query the lookup table directly, call `gnfi_query()` with the settings used
by `view_lookup()`:

```{r lookup-using-gnfi-query, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
federal_states <- gnfi_query(
  table = "lookup_state",
  params = list(select = "*", order = "code,id"),
  accept_profile = "lookup"
)

head(federal_states)
```

Unlike `view_lookup()`, this call requires the full table name, including the
`lookup_` prefix, and explicitly selects the `lookup` API schema through
`accept_profile`.
